title: How to Win People Over
author: The Mindful Manager
summary: Writing as an experienced manager and negotiator, the author uses a Dragons' Den pitch in which an investor doubled her offer for the same stake to ask what makes a negotiation succeed. His answer is that success depends on understanding the person across the table and on creating value for both sides. He applies this to leadership through two hypothetical executives, Amy and Nick, who hold the same title but are motivated by promotion and by learning respectively, so the same request needs a different case for each. Two rules follow: create value for both sides and think beyond the immediate deal. Keeping promises matters because a persuaded colleague who sees unfulfilled promises will stop trusting you, so leaders must deliver the visibility, learning or recognition they used to win agreement. He closes by warning leaders not to use their knowledge of people merely to extract more from them.
points: A better question than how to win a negotiation is what has to happen for everyone to feel they got a good deal.
Getting someone to do something differs from getting them on board, and the second depends on understanding what motivates that particular person.
Two colleagues with the same title can need different pitches, such as visibility for the ambitious one and skill development for the learner.
A deal that leaves the other side feeling pressured damages the relationship and the effort they give next time.
Leaders must follow through on what they promised and recognise the contribution, or the arrangement turns into a sense of being taken advantage of.
quotes: Perhaps the better question isn’t how to win a negotiation, but what needs to happen for everyone to feel they’ve got a good deal.
In these situations, there’s a difference between getting someone to do something and getting them genuinely on board.
But what if, instead of focusing on how to get them to do the work, you focused on why they might want to do it?
The point isn’t to tell people what they want to hear. It’s to understand what matters to them well enough to find a solution that works for both of you.
If they felt pressured into accepting a price that wasn’t worthwhile for them, they might be less keen to work with you again or put less effort into the relationship if they do.
If you persuade Amy to take on the extra work by promising her exposure to senior stakeholders, make sure those introductions happen.
We need to be careful not to use that understanding simply to get more out of them.

Winning people over isn’t about finding the perfect argument, pushing harder or having the last word. It’s about understanding the person in front of you, finding a way forward that benefits both of you and leaving them feeling they would happily work with you again.
